headline: Springs building toward the new moon push porgies deep and fluke into the guts
subhead: Shelter Island scup are stacked and biting hard while summer heat shoves the fluke out of the flats and into the channels.
body_markdown:
Last week the Peconic did what it always does in early July — it warmed up fast and quiet, no big blow to stir it, just sun and slack air pushing the surface temps into the upper 70s across the flats. Robins Island shoal and the west side of Little Peconic were baking by midweek, and that heat did exactly what warm shallow water always does this time of year: it pushed the fluke off the sand and into anything with current and depth. We're in the same pattern the South Shore guys are seeing in Great South Bay right now — bay water pushing fish toward the channels and inlets — except our version of an inlet is Plum Gut, the North Ferry channel, and the cut off Jessup's Neck. The moon's waning toward new, which means the tides have been building all week and will keep building into the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current, and that's the piece that matters most right now.

This coming week we're heading into full spring tides ahead of the new moon around the middle of the month, with the strongest exchange stacking up Friday through Monday. That's going to sharpen the bite at every rip and cut in this zone. More water moving through Plum Gut and the Shelter Island ferry channels means more bait getting pushed and pulled, which means bass and blues stacking on the edges to ambush it, and porgies and fluke settling into the seams where the current slows just enough to feed without burning energy. If you fish moving water for a living like I do, spring tides are when you want to be on the water, not neaps — the fish get lazy and predictable on neaps. Right now they've got no choice but to eat on the clock.

Porgies are the story of the summer so far, and Shelter Island is still the epicenter. Cedar Island and the flats off Coecles Harbor have been stacked with scup in the 12 to 15-inch class, some pushing 16, biting best on the last two hours of the incoming into high, in 15 to 22 feet of water. Small hooks, half a sandworm or a chunk of clam on a simple high-low rig with just enough weight to hold bottom — that's all you need. Don't overcomplicate it. The bite window tightens right around the tide change, so if you're anchored up off Nine Mile Point or drifting the flats south of Barcelona, be ready the last hour before the top and the first hour of the drop. Orient Point has also been kicking out solid scup for the boats working the rockier bottom off the lighthouse grounds, though that spot fishes better with a little chop to keep the bait moving.

Fluke have thinned out in the open bay flats — Noyack Bay's shallow water got too warm to hold them consistently — but the channel edges are producing. The deeper cut running between North Haven and Shelter Island, and the drop-off in the Three Mile Harbor channel, have both been giving up keeper fluke in the 20 to 21-inch range on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with a squid strip, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the outgoing tide in 25 to 35 feet. The deeper water in the Gut itself, right where it necks down before Orient Point, has been worth a drift too, though you need to time it — that current runs hard on the bigger tides we're heading into, and a light bucktail just gets swept off bottom. Bump up to an ounce or more through the peak of the outgoing there.

Striped bass have been a mixed bag — some good mornings, some quiet ones. The better action has come at first light working bunker schools pushed up against the Shelter Island shoreline near Cedar Point and out toward Gardiners Island, blues mixed in and chopping the pods on the surface. Topwater plugs and bucktails worked through the edges of the bait have taken fish to the mid-20-inch range, with the occasional bigger bass grabbing a chunk of fresh bunker fished on the bottom near the drop-offs. It's not a blitz every day — some mornings the bunker sit tight and don't get worked at all — but when the bass do show, they're eating well. I'd rather find a nervous bunker school at dawn than blind-cast open water right now.

Weakfish, I have to be honest, are still a ghost around here. The water's warm enough — well above the old 70-degree benchmark everyone used to point to — but warm water alone isn't bringing them back. I haven't heard of a single legitimate weak this month anywhere in the bay, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

Looking ahead, I'd focus the weekend around the building spring tides. If the wind stays light through Saturday and Sunday, I'd fish the Shelter Island channels on the outgoing for fluke, then slide over to the Cedar Island flats for the last of the incoming porgy bite. Monday's tides will be close to peak strength for the cycle — that's when I'd bet on the bass showing at dawn along the bunker pods, because bigger current means bigger bait movement, and bigger bait movement is what wakes these fish up.
